items.title: When courts are too slow, police replace judges
items.syllabus: GS2 › Structure, organisation and functioning of the judiciary; Police reforms · GS4 › Probity in governance
items.context: Abhinav Chandrachud argues that years-long civil suits push well-connected litigants to the police, who turn debt and contract disputes into criminal cases of 'cheating' or 'breach of trust'. This creates a parallel, coercive civil-justice system.
ideas: Delay breeds a 'parallel justice' system: police summons and threats of arrest replace a court's verdict.
GS2 · Pendency / police reforms
Judicial delay has bred 'parallel justice', with police summons and arrest threats replacing a court's verdict in civil disputes.
The root is too few judges: about 15 per million people in Maharashtra against about 157 in New York state.
GS2 · Judicial vacancies
Maharashtra has about 15 judges per million people against about 157 in New York state; vacancies feed delay.
Using criminal law to settle a civil debt is abuse of process; the Supreme Court has discouraged it, but practice lags the law.
GS2 rule of law · GS4 probity
Turning a civil debt into a criminal case is abuse of process, discouraged by the Supreme Court but common in practice.
keywords: Turning debt or contract quarrels into 'cheating' cases
The criminalisation of civil disputes shows police discretion being misused for private ends.
Using legal procedure for an improper aim
Using criminal law to recover a debt is a textbook abuse of process.
Delay itself defeats the purpose of justice
A Bombay HC suit filed in 1947 settled only in 2026: justice delayed is justice denied.
Law in the books vs law in action
The gap between what the law says and how it works
Reform must close the gap between law in the books and law in action.
data: Judges per million people: Maharashtra vs New York state
With about 15 judges per million in Maharashtra against about 157 in New York state, India's courts are short-staffed.
A Bombay HC suit filed in 1947, settled only this year
A Bombay High Court suit filed in 1947 was settled only after 79 years.
examples: When courts fail him, the undertaker turns to the mafia don; the author uses it to show why people seek other routes
As in The Godfather, when courts fail, citizens turn to other, often coercive, sources of 'justice'.
The officer who refuses an influential complainant
The author notes that not every officer gives in to pressure
An officer who refuses an influential complainant's pressure upholds impartiality and the rule of law.
pyqs: Free legal aid is not enough if justice takes decades: cite the 79-year Bombay HC suit and ~15 judges per million in Maharashtra against ~157 in New York state.
Argue for Lok Adalats and ADR: when civil suits take 20+ years, settlements move to police stations instead.
Rule of law: 'law on the books' versus 'law in action' when police turn debt disputes into criminal cases.
The police-as-debt-collector trend shows why probity matters for governance and public trust.
items.summary: Slow civil courts are pushing creditors to the police, who turn money disputes into criminal cases to force a settlement (Abhinav Chandrachud).
evolution: The Privy Council observed that a litigant's troubles in India begin when he has obtained a decree.
A Bombay High Court suit took 79 years before it was settled out of court.

items.title: Keralam passes India's first state law to protect senior citizens' rights
items.syllabus: GS2 › Welfare schemes and laws for vulnerable sections · GS1 › Population and demographic transition · GS4 › Compassion towards the weaker sections
items.context: The Keralam Assembly passed the Senior Citizens (Care and Protection of Rights) Bill, 2026, the first state-level legal framework for elder welfare. It makes elder care rights-based, regulated and professional.
ideas: Elder care moves from charity and family duty to rights backed by the state.
GS2 · Vulnerable sections
Keralam's 2026 law moves elder care from charity to enforceable rights.
Ageing in place: care at home first, institutions as the last resort.
GS1 · Ageing and family
With joint families shrinking, 'ageing in place', care at home first, is the humane model.
The care economy needs standards: regulated care homes and certified caregivers.
GS2 social sector · GS3 jobs
Regulated care homes and certified caregivers can turn the care economy into decent jobs.
keywords: Welfare as an entitlement, not a favour
A rights-based approach treats welfare as an entitlement, as Keralam's elder-rights law does.
Older people living independently at home
Keralam's law gives senior citizens the right to age in place, safely at home.
Advance written choice on life-sustaining treatment
Keralam's law recognises living wills, extending dignity to the end of life.
Paid and unpaid work of looking after others
Ageing raises demand for the care economy, much of it unpaid work by women.
examples: Keralam Senior Citizens (Care and Protection of Rights) Bill, 2026
Keralam's Senior Citizens Bill, 2026, India's first state elder-rights law, is a model for other ageing states.
pyqs: Ageing is a core challenge of the demographic transition; Keralam's law is a policy response.
As family support weakens, the state steps in with a rights framework for the aged.
The Bill recognises living wills for senior citizens, linking to the passive-euthanasia debate.
items.summary: Keralam passed India's first state law giving senior citizens enforceable rights: to age at home, to make living wills, and to regulated care.
evolution: Central Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act focused on maintenance by children (background, not from the report).
Keralam moves to a rights-based law covering care standards, caregivers and living wills.

items.title: China says it is strictly abiding by pacts with India amid LAC face-offs in Arunachal
items.syllabus: GS2 › India and its neighbourhood · GS3 › Security challenges in border areas
items.context: Days after the ITBP chief spoke of face-offs at several locations in Arunachal Pradesh, China said it strictly abides by agreements and conducts normal patrols. India's MEA said friction occurs when Chinese forces depart from established patrolling patterns in border pockets.
ideas: Normalisation since Galwan is real but fragile: friction on the ground keeps returning.
GS2 · India–China
Six years after Galwan, India–China normalisation remains fragile as face-offs recur along the LAC.
Dialogue at many levels (Corps Commander, diplomatic, leaders) keeps small incidents from escalating.
GS2/GS3 · Border management
Multi-level talks, from Corps Commanders to leaders, keep LAC incidents from escalating.
keywords: A persistent trust deficit outlasts every India–China border agreement.
The three stages of easing a military stand-off
Disengagement must be followed by de-escalation and de-induction for real peace on the LAC.
Steps that reduce the risk of miscalculation
Confidence-building measures reduce the risk of 'misunderstanding and miscalculation' on the LAC.
Ties must rest on the 'three mutuals': mutual respect, sensitivity and interest.
examples: Deadly clash followed by a stand-off of over four years
The 2020 Galwan clash was followed by a military stand-off of over four years.
pyqs: Recurring face-offs in Arunachal show why border infrastructure and the ITBP's role on the China border matter.
Border management needs mechanisms like Corps Commander talks to avoid 'misunderstanding and miscalculation'.
items.summary: Fresh face-offs in Arunachal Pradesh: China says it follows the border pacts; India says friction comes when Chinese patrols depart from agreed patterns.
evolution: Deadly Galwan clashes, followed by a military face-off that lasted over four years.
Last two years
Both sides took measures to rebuild relations.
Corps Commander talks at the Wacha-Damai border meeting point.
Sep 2026
Modi and Xi met at the BRICS summit in New Delhi; Modi stressed the 'three mutuals'.
Oct 2026
Fresh face-offs reported in Arunachal.

items.title: To ease energy transition, ramp up storage, strengthen transmission
items.syllabus: GS3 › Infrastructure: energy; Investment models; Conservation
items.context: A former CEA member writes that India has moved from chronic power deficits to a solar-hour glut and night-time deficits. The answer, he argues, is storage, stronger transmission, demand-side management and markets that reward flexibility.
ideas: Capacity is not the goal; power when people need it, by night as well as by day, is.
GS3 · Energy transition
India has moved from shortages to a solar-hour surplus, but night-time deficits show capacity is not enough.
Storage is the bottleneck: pumped storage is slow to build and bid prices are said to be unremunerative.
GS3 · Infrastructure
Storage is the bottleneck of India's energy transition; pumped storage is slow to build.
Wasted solar power and constant ramping of coal plants are a double loss.
GS3 · Resource efficiency
Curtailed solar and constant ramping of coal plants are a double loss for the grid.
keywords: Midday solar glut, evening demand peak
India's grid now faces a duck curve: a midday solar glut and an evening demand peak.
Clean power supplied at all hours
Storage and transmission are needed to deliver round-the-clock clean power.
Forcing generators to cut output the grid cannot absorb
Without storage, solar power is curtailed, wasting cheap clean energy.
Shifting or cutting demand to balance the grid
Demand-side management can shift use to solar hours and ease the evening peak.
data: Renewable capacity incl. large hydro, and its share of the total
Renewables, including large hydro, are about 292 GW, roughly 53% of India's installed capacity.
India's solar capacity has reached about 162 GW.
Thirty years ago 40% of Indians had no electricity (World Bank); today India has a daytime surplus.
pyqs: Capacity is not the only target: a solar-hour glut with night deficits shows storage and transmission are the bottleneck.
Grid flexibility and storage as part of energy security.
Cheap solar now forces coal plants to ramp up and down, shortening their life.
items.where: The Editorial Page, page 12 (Somit Dasgupta (teaser on page 1))
items.summary: India now has surplus power in solar hours and shortages at night; a former CEA member argues storage and transmission are the missing pieces.
evolution: 30 years ago
40% of Indians had no electricity (World Bank, cited in the article).
Electricity Act allowed state electricity boards to be split into separate companies.
Around 2008
Power exchanges in Delhi and Mumbai led to a capacity boom; over 1,00,000 MW of coal capacity added 2010-2020.
About 292 GW renewables (53% of capacity), 162 GW solar; daytime glut, night deficit.

items.title: Govt notifies E100 as auto fuel for flex-fuel vehicles
items.syllabus: GS3 › Infrastructure: energy; Environment (pollution); Agriculture-linked industry
items.context: The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways amended the Central Motor Vehicle Rules to allow flex-fuel vehicles to run on up to E100 (nearly pure ethanol). Ordinary petrol or E20 vehicles cannot use E100.
ideas: Ethanol reduces dependence on imported crude oil.
GS3 · Energy security
Higher ethanol blends such as E100 cut India's dependence on imported crude.
Lower lifecycle emissions are possible, but they depend on the crop and the production process.
GS3 · Environment (balanced view)
Ethanol's climate benefit depends on the crop and process used, so lifecycle emissions must be counted.
keywords: Crops for ethanol compete with crops for food and water
Biofuel policy must manage the food-vs-fuel trade-off over land and water.
Vehicle built to run on different petrol-ethanol blends
Flex-fuel vehicles, now allowed to run on E100, offer a parallel route to cleaner transport alongside EVs.
Emissions across production, transport and use
Judged by lifecycle emissions, not tailpipe alone, biofuels are not automatically green.
Ethanol blending reduces import dependence and the oil import bill.
pyqs: Higher ethanol blends reduce dependence on imported crude.
Flex-fuel vehicles as a parallel route to cleaner transport alongside EVs.
links: Related Explained: Centre clears way for flex-fuel up to E100
items.summary: Flex-fuel vehicles may now run on E100, nearly pure ethanol; ordinary petrol and E20 vehicles cannot.
evolution: Before Oct 2026
Ongoing debate over the use of E20 fuel (as the report notes).
E100 notified, but only for vehicles built as flex-fuel.

items.title: Govt to study hurdles faced by women-led informal businesses
items.syllabus: GS1 › Role of women; Women's issues · GS3 › Employment; Inclusive growth
items.context: The Statistics Ministry plans to add questions to its Annual Survey of Unincorporated Sector Enterprises (ASUSE) on 'women-specific constraints' such as restrictions on time and mobility and household responsibilities.
ideas: What is not measured is rarely fixed; better data is the first step to targeted support for women entrepreneurs.
GS1 women · GS3 inclusive growth
What is not measured is rarely fixed; MoSPI's new survey questions are a first step to supporting women entrepreneurs.
Household and care responsibilities hold back women's work; the gap is widest among the young.
GS3 · Female LFPR
Household and care duties hold back women's work most among the young.
keywords: Too little free time because of unpaid work
Time poverty from unpaid care work keeps India's women out of paid work.
Household and care work that is not paid or counted
Unpaid care work remains invisible in GDP but sustains the economy.
Gender-disaggregated data is the basis of gender-responsive policy.
Share of women working or looking for work
India's female LFPR, at 34.6% against 77.4% for men (PLFS), shows the gender gap in work.
data: Female vs male labour force participation (Sept)
Women's labour force participation is 34.6% against 77.4% for men (PLFS, September).
Among 15–29-year-olds, women's participation is just 21.5% against 61.1% for men.
About 27% of India's informal enterprises are headed by women (ASUSE 2025).
examples: Adding women-specific questions to a national survey
MoSPI's adding women-specific constraints to its enterprise survey shows the state measuring before it fixes.
pyqs: Measuring household responsibilities makes the care burden on women entrepreneurs visible.
Use the LFPR gap (34.6% women vs 77.4% men) to show equity needs targeted support.
27% of informal enterprises are headed by women; informality shapes their constraints.
items.summary: The Statistics Ministry will add questions on women-specific constraints (time, mobility, household duties) to its survey of informal businesses.
evolution: First Annual Survey of Unincorporated Sector Enterprises (ASUSE).
Latest round: 27% of informal enterprises women-headed.
Survey to measure women-specific constraints.

items.title: Climate justice needs quicker compensation: first Loss and Damage payout to Nepal
items.syllabus: GS3 › Environment; Disaster management · GS2 › International institutions; India's neighbourhood · GS4 › Ethical issues in international funding
items.context: The UN's Fund for Loss and Damage has allocated $21.6 million (about Rs 190 crore) to Nepal, nearly two months after devastating floods. It is the first time the Fund has earmarked a grant for a disaster-affected nation. The Indian Express argues the episode should become a case study for reforming the Fund.
ideas: Loss and damage is compensation, not charity, because it rests on responsibility for climate change.
GS3 climate · GS2 global governance
Loss and damage finance is compensation owed, not charity, because it rests on responsibility for emissions.
Speed is justice: delays raise hardship and rebuilding costs, especially for poor countries.
GS3 DM · GS4 fairness
Delayed climate compensation is justice denied: it raises hardship and rebuilding costs.
Money is short: $822 million pledged, about a third of pending claims.
GS3 · Climate finance
The Loss and Damage Fund has only $822 million pledged, about a third of pending claims.
keywords: Climate harm beyond what mitigation and adaptation can prevent
Loss and damage covers harm beyond what mitigation and adaptation can prevent.
Sharing climate burdens by responsibility and capacity
Climate justice demands that burdens be shared by responsibility and capacity.
Common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities
India's climate diplomacy rests on CBDR-RC: common but differentiated responsibilities.
Those who cause harm bear its cost
The polluter pays principle makes loss and damage a duty of high emitters.
data: Nepal emits barely 0.1% of global emissions yet suffers some of the worst climate disasters.
Pledged to the Fund, about a third of pending claims
Pledges of $822 million cover only about a third of pending loss-and-damage claims.
examples: Barely 0.1% of emissions, yet among the hardest hit
Nepal, a low emitter facing high losses, shows why climate justice is a moral question.
An ice-and-rock avalanche set off flash floods and wrecked hydropower plants
Nepal's avalanche-triggered floods show cascading Himalayan hazards that destroy infrastructure.
pyqs: Loss-and-damage finance as part of climate commitments: first grant, $822 million pledged against far larger claims.
Nepal's avalanche-triggered floods as a Himalayan climate hazard with cross-border lessons.
Nepal lost at least 10% of its hydropower facilities: infrastructure in fragile terrain.
Nepal's case shows who pays for 'development' driven by greed: low emitters, high losses.
links: Related Explained (Telegram): Why Rs 190 crore payout to Nepal matters
items.summary: The UN Fund for Loss and Damage made its first grant, to flood-hit Nepal; the Indian Express says payouts must be faster and the Fund reformed.
evolution: Fund for Loss and Damage created at COP27, after a nearly three-decade campaign by vulnerable nations.
Fund operationalised.
First grant earmarked, to Nepal; developed countries insisted it is an exception, not a precedent.
COP31 begins in Antalya, Turkey, with compensation on the agenda.

items.title: Punjab farm fires: why most stubble-burning incidents are in two districts
items.syllabus: GS3 › Environmental pollution; Cropping patterns; Agricultural technology · GS4 › Ethical dilemmas: private gain vs public good
items.context: Punjab has recorded 684 farm fires this season, 457 of them (69%) in Tarn Taran and Amritsar. Early harvesting of short-duration paddy in the Majha region lets farmers fit in a third crop of peas or potatoes before wheat, which leaves little time to clear fields without burning.
ideas: The real cause is the crop calendar, not just a lack of machines.
GS3 · Stubble burning
Stubble burning in Majha is driven by the crop calendar, not merely a lack of machines.
Fires are falling year on year; support and awareness matter as much as penalties.
GS3 policy · GS4 persuasion
Falling farm fires show that support and awareness work alongside penalties.
Leaving the paddy-wheat cycle is the long-term fix (see Manauli's sweet-corn shift).
GS3 · Crop diversification
Moving out of the paddy-wheat cycle, as Manauli did, is the long-term fix for stubble burning.
keywords: Farmers stuck in one crop cycle by MSP and habit
A paddy-wheat lock-in leaves farmers little choice but to burn straw before the next crop.
A private act that imposes costs on others
Stubble burning is a negative externality: a private saving that imposes health costs on millions.
Handling straw in the field / removing it for use elsewhere
In-situ and ex-situ residue management offer alternatives to burning.
Moving to a wider mix of crops
Crop diversification is the durable answer to stubble burning and groundwater stress.
data: Farm fires by this point in the season, 2024 → 2025 → 2026
Punjab's farm fires fell from 1,857 (2024) to 743 (2025) to 684 (2026) by the same point in the season.
Despite 1.25 lakh residue-management machines, Punjab still sees farm fires.
examples: About 70% of 2,000 acres moved from paddy to sweet corn and vegetables; farmers formed an FPO
Manauli in Haryana moved about 70% of its land from paddy to sweet corn and vegetables and formed an FPO.
pyqs: Majha's third crop and Manauli's shift to sweet corn show diversification in practice.
Why farmers choose high-value crops: Manauli's returns and market links.
Farm fires and clean air: 684 fires so far against 743 last year and 1,857 in 2024.
items.summary: Most of Punjab's farm fires this season are in Tarn Taran and Amritsar, where a third crop leaves farmers too little time to clear fields without burning.
evolution: 1,857 fires by this point in the season.
743 fires in the same period.
684 fires so far, but an early spike in Majha.

items.title: Delhi plans a bottle-return scheme, taking a cue from Uttarakhand and Goa
items.syllabus: GS3 › Solid waste management; Conservation · GS4 › Environmental ethics in public administration
items.context: Delhi is considering a Deposit Refund Scheme (DRS) in which consumers pay an extra Re 1 or Rs 2 for a plastic bottle and get it back on return, possibly using QR codes and starting with tourist spots.
ideas: A small refundable deposit changes behaviour more than appeals alone.
GS3 · Waste management
A small refundable deposit changes behaviour more than appeals alone.
It moves people from 'use and throw' to 'use, return and recover': a circular economy.
GS3 environment · Essay
Deposit schemes move citizens from 'use and throw' to 'use, return and recover'.
Environmental ethics in public administration: the state designs incentives so that the right choice becomes the easy one.
GS4 · Environmental ethics
In a deposit scheme the state designs incentives so the environmentally right choice becomes the easy one.
keywords: Changing behaviour through incentives, not orders
A refundable deposit is a nudge: behaviour change without coercion.
Producers made responsible for their products' waste
Extended Producer Responsibility makes producers accountable for their plastic waste.
Reusing and recycling materials to cut waste
A circular economy keeps materials in use and cuts waste.
Refundable deposit on containers to encourage return
Deposit refund schemes, as in Uttarakhand and Goa, raise container returns.
data: Bottle return rate in Uttarakhand after its deposit scheme
Uttarakhand's deposit scheme raised bottle returns from about 20% to nearly 90%.
Delhi govt report, via IE p. 11
Delhi generates about 1,500 tonnes of plastic waste a day.
examples: Won a Digital India Award and was expanded across Uttarakhand
Uttarakhand's Kedarnath deposit refund pilot (2022) won a Digital India Award and was scaled statewide.
pyqs: Directly usable: Delhi's 1,500 tonnes of plastic waste a day, 19% unprocessed, and the deposit-refund fix.
Deposit-refund schemes as a collection model: Uttarakhand's returns rose from about 20% to nearly 90%.
Use the bottle-return scheme as an environmental issue seen through environmental ethics.
items.summary: Delhi plans a refundable deposit on plastic bottles, copying schemes that already work in Uttarakhand and Goa.
evolution: Single-use plastic items banned across India.
Uttarakhand's pilot at Kedarnath; returns rose from about 20-22% to nearly 90%.
Now
Goa runs a Rs 5 deposit; Delhi plans its own scheme.

items.title: Ahead of Cyclone Arnab, Andhra evacuates pregnant women; Odisha deploys ministers
items.syllabus: GS3 › Disaster management · GS4 › Care ethics of the state; Compassion towards the weaker sections
items.context: With the IMD forecasting landfall of Cyclone Arnab on the Andhra Pradesh coast on 28 October, Andhra Pradesh began evacuating vulnerable people, and Odisha banned sea fishing and tourist entry in six districts.
ideas: Good preparedness protects the most vulnerable first, before landfall.
GS3 · DM best practice
Good preparedness protects the most vulnerable first, before landfall.
Many layers act together: early warning, NDRF and SDRF teams, school closures, fishing bans and ministers on the ground.
GS3 · Coordinated response
Early warning, NDRF and SDRF teams, school closures and fishing bans work best together.
The state's ethics of care: planning for those who cannot protect themselves.
GS4 · Ethics of care
Evacuating pregnant women first reflects the state's ethics of care.
keywords: Preparedness aimed at saving every life
Cyclone preparedness should aim at zero casualties, protecting the most vulnerable first.
Identifying who is most at risk before a disaster
Vulnerability mapping lets the state protect those most at risk before disaster strikes.
Moral duty to attend to the needs of the vulnerable
The ethics of care asks administrators to put the most vulnerable first.
National and State Disaster Response Forces
NDRF and SDRF teams pre-positioned before landfall save lives.
examples: Moved to health centres before Cyclone Arnab's landfall
Before Cyclone Arnab, Andhra Pradesh moved 4,711 pregnant women to health centres: gender-sensitive, caring administration.
Eight ministers deputed to oversee cyclone preparedness
Odisha deputed eight ministers to districts to oversee cyclone preparedness, making accountability visible.
pyqs: Proactive rather than reactive: 4,711 pregnant women moved to health centres before landfall.
Resilience means protecting the most vulnerable first; NDRF and SDRF teams in place early.
IMD forecasts and warnings driving early action in Andhra Pradesh and Odisha.
Prioritising pregnant women before landfall: compassion and planning in disaster response.
items.summary: Before Cyclone Arnab's landfall, Andhra Pradesh moved 4,711 pregnant women to hospitals and Odisha sent eight ministers to the districts.

items.title: 'Godzilla' El Niño effects to be felt into 2027: decoding the WMO warning
items.syllabus: GS1 › Important geophysical phenomena; Climatology · GS3 › Food security; Disaster management
items.context: The World Meteorological Organization has warned that the intense 2026 El Niño will peak around year-end and affect weather well into 2027. It has already weakened India's southwest monsoon.
ideas: El Niño weakens the Indian monsoon, causing drought and heatwaves.
GS1 climatology · GS3 drought
El Niño weakens the Indian monsoon, bringing drought and heatwaves.
Effects into 2027 threaten food and water security and could push up fertiliser and fuel prices.
GS3 · Food security
The 2026 El Niño, lasting into 2027, threatens food and water security and could raise fertiliser and fuel prices.
keywords: Preparing farming and water systems to withstand dry years
Drought-proofing farming and water systems is the answer to recurring El Niño years.
Rising food prices after a poor harvest
A weak monsoon feeds food inflation, hurting the poor most.
Farming that relies on rain, not irrigation
Monsoon-dependent agriculture leaves India exposed to every El Niño.
One shock triggering others: drought, prices, water
El Niño brings cascading risks: drought, prices, water shortage.
data: Share of India's annual rain from the southwest monsoon
The southwest monsoon brings about 70% of India's annual rainfall.
India's 2026 monsoon, the fourth driest since 2001
India's 2026 monsoon ended at 87% of the long period average, the fourth driest since 2001.
pyqs: El Niño as a drought driver: the 2026 monsoon ended at 87% of LPA.
WMO warning: an El Niño strong enough to weaken the monsoon and affect weather into 2027.
Effects into 2027 on food and water security.
items.summary: The WMO warns that this year's intense El Niño, which already weakened India's monsoon, will affect weather well into 2027.
evolution: El Niño peaked at 2.3°C (NOAA data, cited in the report).
June 2026
Current El Niño emerged and intensified rapidly.
2026 monsoon
Ended at 87% of LPA, the fourth driest since 2001.
Into 2027
WMO expects effects to continue.

items.title: Microsoft offers voluntary exit to about 60,000 employees, including staff in India
items.syllabus: GS3 › Indian economy: employment; Science and technology: developments and their effects (AI)
items.context: Microsoft announced a 'Voluntary Exit Offer' for eligible employees in the US, Canada, the UK and India, at its experience level 70 or below. About 60,000 people, roughly a quarter of its 223,000 workforce, are eligible. Reports link the move to the company's effort to balance a costly AI infrastructure build-out with capital efficiency.
ideas: Spending is shifting to AI, and big firms are reshaping their workforce around it.
GS3 · Technology and jobs
Big tech is reshaping its workforce to fund AI, as Microsoft's 2026 exit offer shows.
Even voluntary exits shrink jobs; workers need reskilling and social security for the AI era (editor's view).
GS3 · Skilling
Even voluntary exits shrink jobs; India needs reskilling and social security for the AI era.
keywords: AI raises the risk of technological unemployment in white-collar jobs.
Training workers for new or better jobs
Large-scale reskilling and upskilling must keep pace with AI adoption.
Income support for workers between jobs
A social security net must cushion workers displaced by technology.
examples: Big tech trimming staff to fund AI, including in India
Microsoft's 2026 voluntary exit offer, covering staff in India, shows AI-era workforce change.
items.paper: Indian Express Explained (online, shared by you)
items.sources: Facts from CNBC (26 Oct 2026), GeekWire and CBS News. The Indian Express explainer you shared could not be opened here, so its India-specific details are not included.
pyqs: AI is reshaping work: firms are cutting staff to fund AI infrastructure.
Technology-driven job loss as structural unemployment.
India's tech workforce in IT cities is exposed to global restructuring.
links: Indian Express Explained (the link you shared)
items.summary: Microsoft has offered voluntary exit to about a quarter of its workforce, including staff in India, as it spends heavily on AI.
evolution: Spring 2026
Microsoft's first-ever voluntary retirement programme for long-serving US staff (GeekWire).
Wider Voluntary Exit Offer covering four countries including India.

ethics.title: The stubble dilemma in Punjab
ethics.news: Punjab's farm fires are concentrated in two districts where a third crop leaves farmers too little time to clear fields.

ethics.question: As District Collector during the paddy harvest, you find farmers burning stubble because machines arrive too late for their next crop. How will you balance their livelihood with public health?

ethics.link: Attitudes changed through peer example and visible results, not through orders.

ethics.link: Dignity in old age moves from charity to entitlement; the state supports the family's duty rather than replacing it.
ethics.question: Is care of the elderly a family duty or a responsibility of the state? Discuss in the light of dignity and compassion.

ethics.title: Cyclone Arnab: the most vulnerable first
ethics.news: Andhra Pradesh moved 4,711 pregnant women to hospitals before the cyclone; Odisha sent ministers to the districts.
ethics.syllabus: Compassion towards the weaker sections · Accountability and ethical governance
ethics.link: The care ethics of the state, and a best practice in disaster management: plan for those who cannot protect themselves.
ethics.question: 'The ethics of care is the first principle of disaster management.' Discuss with an example.

ethics.title: Counting what women carry
ethics.news: The Statistics Ministry will measure women-specific constraints, such as household duties, in its survey of informal businesses.
ethics.syllabus: Social justice and gender · Evidence-based, ethical governance
ethics.link: What is not measured is rarely addressed: equity begins by making unpaid care work visible.
ethics.question: 'What is not counted does not count.' Discuss in the context of women's unpaid work and public policy.

ethics.title: Two fathers behind two India cricketers
ethics.news: Tilak Varma's and Nitish Kumar Reddy's fathers made quiet sacrifices for years before their sons played for India.
ethics.syllabus: Role of family in inculcating values
ethics.link: Family is the first school of values: commitment and perseverance are learnt by watching parents.
ethics.question: How does the family shape values such as perseverance and commitment? Illustrate with examples.

essay.title: Jogen Chowdhury: refugee to master painter
essay.text: Born into a landed family in Faridpur in pre-Partition East Bengal, he suffered a great reversal of fortune and became a post-Partition refugee in Calcutta. Drawing on memories of the kantha embroidery and alpona floor art of Bengal's village women, he built a personal modern idiom. The tribute calls him a 'hard optimist' and a 'dreamer of institutions'.
essay.use: For 'A thorn is a changed bud', 'Best lessons are learnt through bitter experiences' and 'magical in the mundane' (art from folk floor drawings).

essay.title: Nepal and the first loss-and-damage grant
essay.text: Nepal accounts for barely 0.1% of global emissions, yet floods triggered by an ice-and-rock avalanche claimed more than 1,400 lives and destroyed at least 10% of its hydropower facilities. Developed countries agreed to the grant only after insisting it be treated as an exception, not a precedent.
essay.use: Our suggested link: a contemporary illustration of 'When two elephants fight, it is the grass that gets trampled', and of justice versus charity (compensation, not aid).

essay.title: Lycurgus Cup and Roman concrete: the science in 'magic'
essay.text: A 1,600-year-old Roman cup glows red in normal light and green when lit from behind. Scientists have only now reverse-engineered it. Roman concrete is still not fully recreated, and Indus Valley drainage still has lessons for cities. The editorial argues that the past's real magic is useful achievement, not myths of flying chariots.
essay.use: For 'magical in the mundane', 'The doubter is a true man of science' (versus pseudo-history) and 'Culture is what we are, civilisation is what we have'.

essay.title: The farmer who copied a friend's strawberries
essay.text: In Manauli, Sonipat, Arun Chauhan switched from paddy to sweet corn after visiting a friend's strawberry farm. His village moved 70% of its land to sweet corn and vegetables, formed an FPO and now sells directly to e-commerce firms.
essay.use: For 'The cost of being wrong is less than the cost of doing nothing', 'Ideas with large consequences are simple' and 'A ship in harbour is safe'.

essay.title: Two fathers behind two India cricketers
essay.text: Behind Tilak Varma and Nitish Kumar Reddy, who won a T20I for India in New Zealand, stand two fathers who had hard years. Nitish's father, Mutyala Reddy, left a stable job at Hindustan Zinc Limited to support his son's practice in Visakhapatnam. Tilak's father, Nagaraju, an electrician, spent sleepless nights making ends meet so that his son could concentrate on cricket.
essay.use: For the role of parents and family in shaping a child's future: sacrifice made quietly, years before any success is visible. Fits 'Hand that rocks the cradle rules the world' (the family as the first institution).

essay.title: Angkrish Raghuvanshi's maiden century
essay.text: Out for 92 on debut three years ago, then dropped, the 22-year-old admitted doubting whether he would ever score a first-class hundred. He finally made 114 for Mumbai.
essay.use: For 'Best lessons are learnt through bitter experiences' and 'Ships sink because of water that gets into them' (self-doubt as the real threat).

essay.title: FIDE's first survey of women in chess
essay.text: 76% of 672 female respondents from 127 federations reported discrimination or harassment. 44% considered stepping away from chess, and 54% never had a female role model or mentor. India was the largest contributor, with 69 respondents.
essay.use: Fresh data for gender-justice essays ('Patriarchy is the least noticed yet most significant structure...'). The lack of mentors shows 'restrictions' at work.

essay.title: From 'use and throw' to 'use, return and recover'
essay.text: Delhi's planned bottle-deposit scheme. Uttarakhand's version raised bottle return rates from about 20% to nearly 90% with a refundable Rs 10 deposit.
essay.use: For nature and ethics essays: small nudges, big behaviour change ('Ideas with large consequences are simple').

essay.title: Ageing with dignity: Keralam's elder-rights law
essay.text: Keralam's new law gives senior citizens the right to age at home, recognises living wills, and regulates care homes and caregivers. The Chief Minister called it a realisation that 'our world is changing'.
essay.use: For 'Life is a long journey between human being and being humane', 'The years teach much...' and 'Hand that rocks the cradle' (care work).
